chapter: Lessons with Papa Tio and Helen Edwards
title: Papa Tio's strict lessons, fees and teaching method
summary: Papa Tio sent pupils home if they had not learned the lesson, charged Laurent fifty cents against two dollars from white pupils, and taught counting and solfege.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: I was wondering some more about your lessons with Papa Teo. What did he teach you? Anything special that you can remember?

Well, Papa Teo was very good. He taught, he taught you all kinds of, uh, Peiju was, uh, he taught you how to master your cards. He taught you, you, different keys that you could pick up, a number so easy. You'd pick up a number so easy. He'd teach you the cards that you could pick up easily. You wouldn't have any trouble and difficulty picking up a number. And, uh, he always would, uh, be very careful in what you were playing. He could sit down there or sit down in the kitchen in the front room and let you be playing, you know, lesson back here. And if you just did that, he got you, he'd come right back and tell you, start over again, watch this measure right here. Tell you where you fumbled it.
Is it quite, very strict? Oh, yeah. Hold on. Wouldn't take your money.

No, you go there, you go there, you pick up your instruments, you put up your music, and you start to playing, and you'd miss one or two notes right off the reel like that. He'd send you home. Don't want your money. Come back when you think you know that lesson. Yeah, come back when you think you know that lesson. When you know that lesson, come back. Don't come back till you know it. That's right. And you didn't want your money.
Not until you could play it. Yeah.
When you play that number, then you'd come back.
About how many lessons a week did you take? One lesson or more? Two. Two a week. Two lessons a week, yeah. What did he charge for the lessons? Do you remember? Well,
he was a friend of mine. He was charging me 50 cents. But he had them boys. He had, when the white band was on his team of capital, he had them. He was getting $2 a lesson from them. $2 a lesson,
yeah.
But he was a friend of mine, you know. Sure. Yeah. Practically always together. And he built his house. I put the shelter over his head for nothing. You understand?
That was a whole lot, you see. So naturally,

he was trying to favor me a little bit. Because he come over to my side, I said, well, don't worry about it. I'm going to charge you. It won't be that much. So I gave him 50 cents on a dollar. That's the most I would pay for, less than a dollar.
Do you remember if Papa Teo had any special way of counting to teach you to count? Did you pat your foot?
Yeah. One, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, one, two,
four. You bring the foot down on one and to the left on two, to the right on three, and up on four. Tom Albert said he was taught that way too. Yeah.
That's the way he was. See then, later on, they used to teach.
Did you have to learn to sing some of those things before you'd play them? Yeah.
Do, re,
mi, fa, so, stuff
You had to go like that with it. The understated with CDFGBC after, later years after, but always in my teenage years there was always Do Re Mi Fa So La Ti Do. I think yes.
Really give you strict training.
